title: He Unlocked the Chains of the Mentally Ill, Then Forged Psychological Ones
dek: Pinel cut Bicêtre's annual mortality rate from 50% to under 13% in a single year, largely through cleanliness; but he denied organic brain causes, and Foucault accused him of replacing iron chains with psychological ones.
why: A crossover case of medical history and social reform, suited to anyone who wants to see how a humanitarian reform gets amplified by institutions; but the controversy only arrives in the back half, and the early biography is flat.
who: Listeners interested in medical history, the history of psychiatry, social reform and institutional design; founders and policy observers who want to understand how a humanitarian reform gets amplified by institutions and then criticized.
skip: The last roughly three minutes are a listener letter about a dog chewing the floor, unrelated to the topic.

points.h: Having no license is what forced the case-file system into being
points.body: The medical degree Pinel earned in Toulouse only allowed him to practice in Toulouse, so once he reached Montpellier and then Paris he could not practice directly. During his four years in Montpellier he instead visited hospitals repeatedly, talked with patients at length, and took copious notes, organizing the information into detailed records. Because he followed the same group of patients over a long period, he could observe how illnesses evolved and thereby identify patterns in their course. This ‘observe—record—track’ method was later carried to Bicêtre, where it became the prototype for building a file on every patient, recording age, temperature, diagnosis, and even comparing patients' body temperatures against the temperature of the building.

points.h: Classifying the mentally ill with plant taxonomy
points.body: The seventh ward at Bicêtre held 200 men judged to be mentally deranged, many chained in extremely small rooms with only enough chain to shuffle around inside. Pinel communicated closely with the superintendent, Jean-Baptiste Poussin, gathered as much information on patients as possible, organized it into tables, and transferred his knowledge of plant classification over to the problem, trying to build finer diagnostic categories rather than simply lumping people together as ‘mad’. He did not call patients ‘mad’ or ‘insane’ but said they were in a state of ‘mental alienation’—that is, estranged from their own reason.

Pinel put a concrete set of practices in place at Bicêtre: moving patients out of prison-style confinement and into rooms with as much natural light as possible; no longer using chaining as a routine measure; establishing hygiene standards for the institution; having patients take regular hot baths; and providing what today would be called occupational therapy to help patients overcome the obstacles of daily life. Within a year, the institution's annual patient mortality rate fell from 50% to under 13%. The show states plainly that this was largely just a matter of keeping patients and their environment clean—where disease is spreading, without cleanliness there is no control. In addition, a considerable share of patients were able to return to life outside the institution, whereas for most people entering an asylum at the time, the expectation was to die inside it.

points.h: He measured skulls to prove phrenology was garbage
points.body: Pinel recorded age, temperature and diagnosis for every patient, and also measured skulls. This was not because he believed in phrenology—quite the opposite: phrenology was just taking shape during his main working period, built on the craniology that originated in Austria in the 1790s, which held that the shape of a head revealed a person's tendency to violence or madness. Pinel considered the whole thing useless, and he collected skull measurements precisely in order to falsify it. He later wrote that the data seemed to confirm his earlier view: strong mental emotions are the most common cause of mental derangement, and the skulls of the insane have no special conformation that cannot be found in any other skull picked at random.

points.h: He did not unlock everyone's chains
points.body: The image of ‘Pinel breaking all his patients' chains and turning prisoners into patients’ needs discounting. A famous late-19th-century painting by Tony Robert-Fleury depicts him striking off chains, and it shows the women's institution. But he did not release every patient bound in irons: where he judged that loosening them would create danger, patients remained confined and tethered. In the paper he read in 1794 he gave several cases of men he called ‘agitated and violent’, one of whom had been chained for more than forty years. He described their behavior in detail to explain why irons were needed, and wrote that one of the basic principles for dealing with the mentally deranged is ‘a judicious mixture of affability and firmness’, avoiding unnecessary coercion and using only as much force as suffices to restrain them.

points.h: He denied brain pathology, and that is a real flaw
points.body: One of the long-standing criticisms of Pinel's work is that he ignored the physiological causes of mental health problems. His writing discusses at length how life events worsen mental conditions, yet never considers bodily causes—which is strange, because writing on the physiological causes of mental illness goes back to Hippocrates and Galen, and in Pinel's own time Lavoisier, along with his university colleague Michel-Augustin Theret, were already discussing brain chemistry. In 1801 Pinel explicitly argued against bodily causes of madness, writing that ‘the derangement of the understanding is generally considered the result of an organic lesion of the brain, and consequently incurable, a supposition contradicted in a great number of instances by anatomical facts’. The show says directly: he was completely wrong on this point.

points.h: That ‘Citizen, I am convinced’ story may be invented
points.body: In 1849 Chambers' Edinburgh Journal published a story about Pinel, sourced to Pinel's son Scipion Pinel—who also became a psychiatrist. The story goes that during the Terror, a Paris Commune official, Georges Coudon, came to Bicêtre hunting for ‘traitors feigning madness’, and after seeing the chains, the filth and the mad howling with his own eyes, asked Pinel whether it was he who was mad for wanting to unchain these people. Pinel is said to have replied: ‘Citizen, I am convinced that these madmen became so unmanageable only because they were deprived of air and liberty.’ The show says this sounds very cool and clever, but whether the story is true we do not know—it may be family legend, or an editor's invention. It certainly added bricks to Pinel's 19th-century legend.

points.h: Foucault: the iron chains were swapped for psychological ones
points.body: Pinel's writing and work have been argued over almost continuously for nearly two hundred years. Supporters point out how progressive his work was and how many of his ideas remain relevant today. One particularly forceful critic was the 20th-century philosopher Michel Foucault. Foucault argued that Pinel may have removed the physical shackles from patients, but only replaced them with psychological shackles, describing his work as a form of ‘moral imprisonment’ in which patients were manipulated in subtler ways during treatment. By Foucault's logic, in becoming obedient to the doctor, patients became estranged from themselves. The show also notes that this line of Foucault's argument has problems of its own.

It is for this reason that Pinel is not truly modern. Pinel has sometimes been praised as a practical man who had too much sense to waste time spinning philosophical systems. To praise him thus is to praise him for his defects.
